topic: L1.4 Approximation, Standard Form, and Error Analysis
subject: Maths

concepts.name: Significant Figures and Rounding
concepts.description: Counting significant figures in measured values (including leading zeros, trailing zeros, and zeros between digits), rounding to a specified number of decimal places or significant figures, and distinguishing between truncation and rounding.
core_skills: Identify the number of significant figures in a given measurement
Round numbers to a specified number of decimal places or significant figures
Distinguish between truncation and rounding and compute the difference between them
misconceptions: Leading zeros are counted as significant figures
Trailing zeros in a number without a decimal point are always significant
Truncation and rounding always give the same result
traps: Measurements like 0.004050 where leading zeros are not significant but trailing zero after decimal is significant
Rounding vs truncating to 2 decimal places can produce small differences
concepts.depth_test: Given a measurement such as 0.05040, identify the correct number of significant figures and explain why, distinguishing which digits are significant and which are not.

concepts.name: Standard Form (Scientific Notation)
concepts.description: Writing numbers in the form A × 10^n where 1 ≤ |A| < 10 and n is an integer, including very large and very small numbers, and converting between standard form and ordinary decimal representation.
core_skills: Convert large numbers to standard form A × 10^n with 1 ≤ |A| < 10
Convert small decimal numbers (less than 1) to standard form with negative exponents
Convert numbers from standard form back to ordinary decimal representation
Round numbers to specified significant figures when expressing in standard form
misconceptions: The coefficient A must always be an integer
Numbers less than 1 cannot be written in standard form
A coefficient like 45.6 × 10^-9 is in proper standard form
traps: Normalizing coefficients so that 1 ≤ |A| < 10 (e.g., adjusting the exponent when moving the decimal point)
Rounding to 3 significant figures when converting very large numbers to standard form
concepts.depth_test: Convert a very small number like 0.0000000456 to proper normalized standard form A × 10^n with 1 ≤ |A| < 10, explaining why normalization is required.

concepts.name: Calculations in Standard Form
concepts.description: Performing arithmetic operations on numbers expressed in standard form, including multiplication, division, addition, and subtraction, with proper normalization of the final answer.
core_skills: Multiply and divide numbers in standard form using exponent rules
Add and subtract numbers in standard form by first expressing them with the same exponent
Normalize the final result to proper standard form A × 10^n with 1 ≤ |A| < 10
misconceptions: When adding numbers in standard form, exponents can be added directly
When multiplying, coefficients and exponents are treated the same way
An unnormalized result like 12.75 × 10^3 is acceptable as final answer
traps: Adding/subtracting numbers with different powers of 10 requires rewriting with a common exponent
Adjusting both coefficient and exponent during normalization after addition/subtraction
concepts.depth_test: Evaluate (3.5 × 10^8) - (8.0 × 10^7) and explain the steps to obtain a normalized standard form answer, justifying why exponents must be aligned before subtracting.

concepts.name: Absolute, Relative, and Percentage Errors
concepts.description: Defining and calculating absolute error (difference between measured/estimated and true value), relative error, and percentage error for single measurements or estimates.
core_skills: Calculate absolute error given true and measured/estimated values
Calculate percentage (relative) error
Express percentage error to an appropriate number of decimal places
misconceptions: Absolute error is always positive in a certain form regardless of direction
Percentage error uses measured value in the denominator rather than true/accepted value
Sign of error is always ignored
traps: Correctly identifying true (actual) value versus measured/estimated value
Computing percentage error relative to the true value
concepts.depth_test: Given a true value and an estimated/measured value, calculate absolute and percentage error, and explain the distinction between absolute and relative error in terms of what each quantifies.

concepts.name: Error Propagation
concepts.description: Using differential calculus/error propagation rules to determine how uncertainties combine when quantities are added, subtracted, multiplied, divided, or raised to powers. Includes fractional/relative error formulas.
core_skills: Apply the rule that for sums/differences, absolute errors add
Apply the rule that for products/quotients, relative errors add
Apply the power rule: for Z = X^n, the relative error is n × (ΔX/X)
Calculate absolute error from relative error
Express the result in the form value ± Δvalue with appropriate units
misconceptions: When subtracting, relative errors add the same way as for products
Percentage error in radius is the same as percentage error in area of a circle
Errors always cancel out in combinations
traps: For volume V = (4/3)π r^3, percentage error in volume is 3× percentage error in radius
For division R = V/I, both numerator and denominator contribute their relative errors
For squares A = L^2, relative error doubles
For g = 4π^2 L/T^2, the relative error is ΔL/L + 2(ΔT/T)
concepts.depth_test: For g = 4π^2 L/T^2 with measured uncertainties in L and T, derive/state the formula for relative error in g and use it to compute the absolute and percentage error, explaining why the period contributes twice as much as length.

concepts.name: Error Bounds and Measurement Uncertainty
concepts.description: Determining upper and lower bounds for measurements given to a certain precision, computing bounds for calculated quantities, and assessing the effect of intermediate rounding on accuracy.
core_skills: State upper and lower bounds for a measurement given to a specified precision
Calculate upper and lower bounds for derived quantities (e.g., perimeter, area, volume)
Determine maximum possible (worst-case) error from bounds
Compare the effects of rounding at intermediate steps versus rounding only the final result
misconceptions: The bound is always exactly ±half the unit of precision
Lower bound is always measurement minus uncertainty
Intermediate rounding doesn't affect the final result
traps: For measurements to nearest centimeter, the true value lies in [x-0.5, x+0.5) cm
When multiplying, maximum occurs at upper bounds of factors that increase product
Repeated rounding at each intermediate step can accumulate errors (compounding drift)
concepts.depth_test: For a rectangle with length and width measured to nearest centimeter, find upper/lower bounds for perimeter and explain why intermediate rounding can lead to greater accumulated error than rounding only at the end.

concepts.name: Numerical Approximation Techniques
concepts.description: Using approximation methods such as binomial approximation (1+x)^r ≈ 1 + rx for small |x|, linear approximation via differentials, and applying them to estimate values without calculators.
core_skills: Apply binomial approximation (1+x)^r ≈ 1 + rx for |x| << 1
Reformulate expressions into the form (1+x)^r to apply binomial approximation
Use differential approximation to estimate small changes
Compute absolute and percentage error of an approximation
misconceptions: Binomial approximation works for any x regardless of magnitude
The approximation error is negligible for all practical purposes
Linear approximation gives exact results
traps: Recasting numbers like 10001^3 into (10^4 + 1)^3 = 10^12(1 + 10^-4)^3 to get small x
Computing the true value to determine approximation error
concepts.depth_test: Use binomial approximation (1+x)^r ≈ 1 + rx to approximate 10001^3, compute the exact value, and determine both absolute and percentage error of the approximation.
